lesson.menu_title: Maria Claudia in Charge -- Leading the Meeting
lesson.menu_desc: Run the quarterly board meeting yourself: polite requests with would you mind + -ing and could you + base verb, indirect questions in statement word order, and the vocabulary of the chair -- convene, steer, digress, interject, show of hands, motion -- 27 slides
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 21 -- Maria Claudia in Charge -- Leading the Meeting
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Maria Claudia Curimbaba | Lesson 21 -- Leading the Meeting
lesson.grammar_point: polite requests and indirect questions (would you mind + -ing / could you)

listenings.text: Maria Claudia, I want to ask you something before Thursday. I have to be in Houston that morning, so I would like you to chair the quarterly meeting. And honestly, the board should hear the strategy from the person who built it, not from me. A few practical points. First, the clock. The meeting must not overrun, because the call with the Houston lawyers starts at eleven sharp, and counsel joins us at ten. Second, the room. Your uncle will start a sidebar about the port within twenty minutes, he always does. When that happens, steer everyone back to the agenda politely and park the sidebar for after the meeting. It is not rude; it is the job. Third, the decisions. Close every item, even the small ones. A show of hands is enough for most of them, and when the item is a budget decision, put it to the board as a formal motion so the minutes are clean. One last thing. You do not have to sound hard to be firm. Ask instead of ordering, and nobody in that room will notice you are running them.

It is seven in the morning and I am rehearsing the hour ahead. I have decided that I will never give a bare order in that room. Send me the file becomes could you send me the file, and it costs me half a second. For the two most senior people at the table I keep the longer form, would you mind, plus the -ing form of the verb, because that one leaves them room to say in a moment without losing anything. Would you mind taking us through the numbers. Not would you mind to take. Mind always takes the -ing. Then there is the question I am afraid to ask, the one about the contract. I will make it indirect. Could you tell me where we stand on the contract. The word order of a statement, so no inversion and no do or does, and nobody feels cross-examined in front of the board. And I will finish on time. A show of hands on each item, a formal motion on the budget, the actions read back out loud, and the meeting closed at ten forty-five.

extra_audio.text: First, you convene the meeting on time and confirm who is in the room and who is on the call. Then, you hand the first item to the right person with a polite request, not with an order: could you take us through the numbers, or would you mind taking us through them. After that, you steer the room back whenever it starts to digress, and you park any sidebar for later. Next, you bring in the people who have not spoken yet, and you invite them to chime in before the vote. Finally, you close the item with a show of hands, or with a formal motion when money is involved, and you move on before the meeting can overrun.
